title: Speculative Sampling Preserves the Target Distribution
text:
Autoregressive generation normally emits one token per target-model invocation. Speculative decoding asks a cheaper draft model to propose several tokens, scores the proposed continuation with one parallel target pass, and accepts the longest valid prefix (Leviathan et al. 2023).
The speed argument is architectural. The correctness argument is probabilistic. The latter is easy to state incorrectly, so this note derives it from the probability mass assigned by the target p and draft q.

title: Speculative Sampling Preserves the Target Distribution
text:
Autoregressive generation normally emits one token per target-model invocation. Speculative decoding asks a cheaper draft model to propose several tokens, scores the proposed continuation with one parallel target pass, and accepts the longest valid prefix (Leviathan et al. 2023).
The speed argument is architectural. The correctness argument is probabilistic. The latter is easy to state incorrectly, so this note derives it from the probability mass assigned by the target p and draft q.

title: Speculative Sampling Preserves the Target Distribution
text:
One-token acceptance rule
Draw a candidate x\sim q. Accept it with probability

a(x)=\min\left(1,\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}\right).

If it is rejected, sample a replacement from

r(x)=\frac{[p(x)-q(x)]_+}{Z},
\qquad
Z=\sum_y[p(y)-q(y)]_+,
\tag{1}
where [z]_+=\max(0,z). The accepted candidate contributes mass

q(x)a(x)=\min(q(x),p(x)).
\tag{2}
The probability of rejection is

1-\sum_x\min(p(x),q(x))
=\sum_x[p(x)-q(x)]_+
=Z.
\tag{3}
Therefore the final mass at token x is

\underbrace{\min(p(x),q(x))}_{\text{accepted draft}}
+\underbrace{Zr(x)}_{\text{replacement}}
=\min(p(x),q(x))+[p(x)-q(x)]_+
=p(x).

The output is exactly distributed as the target for any draft distribution. A poor draft reduces speed through more rejections, but it does not bias the sample if the residual correction in Equation 1 is implemented correctly.

title: Speculative Sampling Preserves the Target Distribution
text:
Acceptance is distribution overlap
The expected acceptance probability is

\alpha=\sum_xq(x)a(x)=\sum_x\min(p(x),q(x)).
\tag{4}
Using \sum_x p(x)=\sum_xq(x)=1,

\alpha=1-\frac{1}{2}\|p-q\|_1.

Speculative performance is controlled by total-variation distance, not by whether the draft has the same argmax alone.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

p = np.array([0.36, 0.25, 0.17, 0.10, 0.08, 0.04])
q = np.array([0.20, 0.35, 0.10, 0.18, 0.05, 0.12])
accepted = np.minimum(p, q)
residual_mass = np.maximum(p - q, 0)
x = np.arange(len(p))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.7))
ax.bar(x, accepted, label="accepted draft mass")
ax.bar(x, residual_mass, bottom=accepted, label="residual correction")
ax.plot(x, p, "ko", label="target probability")
ax.set(xlabel="token id", ylabel="probability mass", xticks=x)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Accepted draft mass and residual correction for a six-token example. The two components sum exactly to the target distribution.

title: Speculative Sampling Preserves the Target Distribution
section: Verifying a block of draft tokens
text:
Verifying a block of draft tokens
Let the draft propose \gamma tokens. The target scores every position in one pass because teacher-forced evaluation is parallel across the proposed sequence. Verification proceeds left to right. At the first rejection, the rejected token and every later draft token are discarded, a correction token is sampled, and a new round begins.
If every proposal is accepted, the target distribution at the next position is already available, so the round can emit one extra target token. Each round therefore produces between 1 and \gamma+1 tokens.
Under the simplifying assumption that acceptances are independent with constant probability \alpha, the expected number of emitted tokens is

E[N]=1+\alpha+\alpha^2+\cdots+\alpha^\gamma
=\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}{1-\alpha}.
\tag{5}
If one draft step costs a fraction c of one target verification, an idealized throughput improvement is

S(\alpha,\gamma,c)
=\frac{1-\alpha^{\gamma+1}}
{(1-\alpha)(1+\gamma c)}.
\tag{6}

gamma = np.arange(1, 17)
c = 0.05

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
for alpha in (0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 0.9):
    speedup = (1 - alpha ** (gamma + 1)) / ((1 - alpha) * (1 + gamma * c))
    ax.plot(gamma, speedup, "o-", ms=3, label=fr"$\alpha={alpha}$")
ax.axhline(1, color="0.55", lw=1, ls=":")
ax.set(xlabel=r"draft length $\gamma$", ylabel="idealized speedup")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 2: Idealized speedup from Equation 5 as speculation length changes. The draft cost is 5 percent of a target invocation.





Longer speculation is not automatically better. When \alpha is modest, the probability of reaching late draft positions falls geometrically while their generation cost remains. The useful \gamma depends jointly on overlap, draft cost, target batch shape, and hardware.

title: Speculative Sampling Preserves the Target Distribution
text:
A reference sampler

import numpy as np

def speculative_sample(p, q, rng):
    """Return one exact sample from categorical target p using proposal q."""
    candidate = rng.choice(len(q), p=q)
    acceptance = min(1.0, p[candidate] / q[candidate])
    if rng.random() < acceptance:
        return candidate

    residual = np.maximum(p - q, 0.0)
    residual /= residual.sum()
    return rng.choice(len(p), p=residual)

Numerical implementations need additional care. Probabilities may be derived from temperature-scaled or truncated logits. The target and draft must apply the same sampling transformation before the acceptance ratio is formed. The residual should be clamped before normalization to remove small negative values caused by rounding.

title: Speculative Sampling Preserves the Target Distribution
text:
Empirical sanity check

rng = np.random.default_rng(23)
draws = 300_000
counts = np.zeros(len(p), dtype=int)

for _ in range(draws):
    counts[speculative_sample(p, q, rng)] += 1

estimate = counts / draws
stderr = np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / draws)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.7))
ax.errorbar(x, estimate, yerr=3 * stderr, fmt="o", capsize=3,
            label="speculative estimate")
ax.plot(x, p, "x", ms=8, label="target")
ax.set(xlabel="token id", ylabel="probability", xticks=x)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 3: Monte Carlo check with 300,000 speculative samples. Error bars show three standard errors under the target multinomial model.





The Monte Carlo test is not a proof, but it is an effective regression test for sign errors, reversed ratios, and incorrect residual normalization.

title: Speculative Sampling Preserves the Target Distribution
text:
Where the speedup comes from
Speculative decoding generally performs more arithmetic than ordinary decoding. It wins when target inference is limited by serial execution or memory bandwidth and the verification pass can score several positions efficiently. The target’s weights and cache state are amortized across multiple accepted tokens.
The original work reports 2 to 3 times acceleration on T5-XXL with identical outputs (Leviathan et al. 2023). That result does not imply the same gain for every model or serving regime. Speculation can lose when the draft is expensive, distributions have low overlap, verification is compute-bound, or the extra temporary state reduces useful batching.






ImportantExactness has a boundary



The guarantee applies to the acceptance and residual rule above. Heuristic acceptance thresholds, lenience, or replacing the residual distribution with the unmodified target distribution change the sampler unless separately proved correct.

title: Speculative Sampling Preserves the Target Distribution
text:
Takeaway
The draft model is a performance hint. Equations Equation 2 and Equation 3 show why it has no authority over the final distribution: accepted overlap plus rejected residual reconstructs the target exactly.

title: Speculative Sampling Preserves the Target Distribution
text:
References


Leviathan, Yaniv, Matan Kalman, and Yossi Matias. 2023. “Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding.” Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 202: 19274–86. https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/leviathan23a.html.

title: Attention, from Logits to Context
text: The compact formula for attention hides three separate operations: a learned similarity metric, a row-wise probability model, and a content lookup. Pulling those pieces apart is useful because most later improvements change only one of them.

title: Attention, from Logits to Context
text:
The operation and its shapes
Let a sequence be represented by X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{\text{model}}}. A single head forms

Q=XW^Q,\qquad K=XW^K,\qquad V=XW^V,

where Q,K\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_k} and V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_v}. Scaled dot-product attention is (Vaswani et al. 2017)

S=\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}},\qquad
P=\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S+M),\qquad
O=PV.
\tag{1}
The score S_{ij} measures how strongly query position i selects key position j. Each row of P is a categorical distribution. The output o_i is therefore a data-dependent convex combination of value vectors.
For causal self-attention, the mask is

M_{ij}=\begin{cases}
0,&j\le i,\\
-\infty,&j>i.
\end{cases}

Adding the mask before softmax makes every illegal probability exactly zero in ideal arithmetic. In finite precision, implementations use either negative infinity or a sufficiently negative representable value.

title: Attention, from Logits to Context
text:
Why divide by \sqrt{d_k}?
Suppose the components of q and k are independent, centered, and have unit variance. Then

\operatorname{Var}(q^\top k)
=\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_{r=1}^{d_k}q_rk_r\right)
=d_k.

The unscaled logit has standard deviation \sqrt{d_k}. As the head dimension grows, the largest logit tends to dominate the softmax, reducing its entropy and concentrating the Jacobian near zero. Scaling restores an order-one logit variance.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
dims = np.array([8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512])
entropy_scaled, entropy_raw = [], []

for d in dims:
    q = rng.normal(size=(400, d))
    k = rng.normal(size=(400, 64, d))
    logits = np.einsum("bd,bnd->bn", q, k)
    for values, scale in ((entropy_raw, 1.0), (entropy_scaled, np.sqrt(d))):
        z = logits / scale
        z -= z.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        p = np.exp(z)
        p /= p.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        values.append(np.mean(-np.sum(p * np.log(p + 1e-30), axis=1)))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.plot(dims, entropy_raw, "o-", label="unscaled")
ax.plot(dims, entropy_scaled, "o-", label=r"scaled by $\sqrt{d_k}$")
ax.axhline(np.log(64), color="0.55", lw=1, ls=":", label="uniform entropy")
ax.set(xscale="log", xlabel=r"head dimension $d_k$", ylabel="entropy (nats)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Mean attention entropy with and without the square-root scaling. Each point averages 400 random attention rows over 64 keys.





The experiment is deliberately distributional rather than model-specific. It isolates the argument behind the normalization in Equation 1: without it, increasing width changes the effective temperature of attention.

title: Attention, from Logits to Context
text:
The softmax Jacobian
For one row p=\operatorname{softmax}(s),

\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial s_j}=p_i(\delta_{ij}-p_j),
\qquad
J_{\text{softmax}}=\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top.

This matrix is positive semidefinite and has a null direction along the all-ones vector. Adding a constant to every logit does not change the distribution. The same invariance explains the standard stable implementation
def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    shifted = x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    weights = np.exp(shifted)
    return weights / weights.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
Subtracting the maximum changes neither P nor the gradient, but prevents overflow in the exponential.

title: Attention, from Logits to Context
section: Multi-head attention is a structured factorization
text:
Multi-head attention is a structured factorization
With h heads,

\operatorname{MHA}(X)
=\operatorname{Concat}(O_1,\ldots,O_h)W^O,

where each O_r has its own projected queries, keys, and values. For the common choice d_k=d_v=d_{\text{model}}/h, the projection and attention FLOP counts remain approximately constant as h changes:

\underbrace{4nd_{\text{model}}^2}_{Q,K,V,O\text{ projections}}
+\underbrace{2n^2d_{\text{model}}}_{QK^\top\text{ and }PV}.

Heads do not provide free capacity. They partition the channel dimension into several learned similarity spaces. Very small d_k constrains each compatibility function, while a single wide head forces one attention distribution to serve every subspace.

title: Attention, from Logits to Context
section: Memory is not the same as arithmetic
text:
Memory is not the same as arithmetic
The two matrix multiplications require O(n^2d) arithmetic. A literal implementation also writes S and P, each with n^2 entries. At sequence length 16,384, one FP16 matrix for one batch-head pair occupies 512 MiB. The quadratic intermediate, not only the quadratic FLOP count, is the systems problem.
This distinction leads directly to IO-aware kernels such as FlashAttention: equation Equation 1 stays unchanged, but its evaluation order is reorganized so that S and P never reside in high-bandwidth memory as complete matrices.

title: Attention, from Logits to Context
section: What the equation does not guarantee
text:
What the equation does not guarantee
Attention weights are conditional routing coefficients, not a causal explanation. A high value of P_{ij} says that value v_j contributes strongly to output o_i under the current parameterization. Residual connections, value projections, later layers, and correlated features complicate any interpretation beyond that statement.
The normalization also creates competition. Increasing one logit decreases other probabilities in the row, even when those keys are unrelated. This coupling is useful for selection, but it means that attention is not a set of independent relevance scores.

title: Attention, from Logits to Context
text:
Practical checks
A minimal implementation should satisfy three invariants:

Every unmasked row sums to one within numerical tolerance.
Masked probabilities are zero.
Shifting a complete score row by any scalar leaves the output unchanged.

Those tests catch axis errors and many masking mistakes before they become training pathologies.

title: Attention, from Logits to Context
text:
References


Vaswani, Ashish, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, et al. 2017. “Attention Is All You Need.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30. https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762.

title: A Paged KV-Cache Allocator, Built from First Principles
text:
Autoregressive decoding reuses the keys and values of every previous token. Caching them avoids a full prefix recomputation, but turns serving capacity into a memory-allocation problem: request lengths are unknown, sequences arrive and finish at different times, and branching decoders share long prefixes.
This project builds a small simulator for two allocation policies:

Contiguous reservation: reserve each request’s declared maximum length.
Paged allocation: allocate fixed-size token blocks only when needed.

The model is intentionally compact. It does not benchmark a GPU kernel. It isolates the allocator mechanism behind PagedAttention and vLLM (Kwon et al. 2023).

title: A Paged KV-Cache Allocator, Built from First Principles
text:
Autoregressive decoding reuses the keys and values of every previous token. Caching them avoids a full prefix recomputation, but turns serving capacity into a memory-allocation problem: request lengths are unknown, sequences arrive and finish at different times, and branching decoders share long prefixes.
This project builds a small simulator for two allocation policies:

Contiguous reservation: reserve each request’s declared maximum length.
Paged allocation: allocate fixed-size token blocks only when needed.

The model is intentionally compact. It does not benchmark a GPU kernel. It isolates the allocator mechanism behind PagedAttention and vLLM (Kwon et al. 2023).

title: A Paged KV-Cache Allocator, Built from First Principles
text:
Cache size
For a decoder with L layers, h_{kv} key/value heads, head dimension d_h, element size b bytes, and T cached tokens, the cache occupies

B_{KV}=2Lh_{kv}d_hTb.
\tag{1}
The factor two accounts for keys and values. For conventional multi-head attention, h_{kv} equals the query-head count. Multi-query and grouped-query attention reduce h_{kv}, which directly reduces the persistent cache.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

tokens = np.arange(0, 32769, 512)
configs = {
    "32L, 32 KV heads, d=128": (32, 32, 128),
    "32L, 8 KV heads, d=128": (32, 8, 128),
    "80L, 8 KV heads, d=128": (80, 8, 128),
}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
for label, (layers, kv_heads, head_dim) in configs.items():
    gib = 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * tokens * 2 / 2**30
    ax.plot(tokens, gib, label=label)
ax.set(xlabel="cached tokens", ylabel="KV cache per request (GiB)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: KV-cache memory per request for three decoder configurations in FP16. Model labels describe layers, KV heads, and head dimension.





Equation Equation 1 is linear in context length and batch size. That is better than storing a quadratic attention matrix, but it becomes the dominant dynamic allocation in a serving engine.

title: A Paged KV-Cache Allocator, Built from First Principles
A Paged KV-Cache Allocator, Built from First Principles
text:
A workload experiment
The following experiment samples 2,000 concurrent requests. Prompt lengths follow a log-normal distribution, maximum generation budgets are deliberately conservative, and actual completions vary. The comparison measures reserved token slots rather than allocator metadata.

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
requests = 2_000
prompt = np.clip(rng.lognormal(mean=5.2, sigma=0.8, size=requests).astype(int), 16, 4096)
budget = rng.choice([128, 256, 512, 1024], size=requests, p=[0.2, 0.35, 0.3, 0.15])
actual = np.array([rng.integers(1, limit + 1) for limit in budget])
live = prompt + actual
block_sizes = np.array([8, 16, 32, 64, 128])

contiguous_reserved = prompt + budget
contiguous_efficiency = live.sum() / contiguous_reserved.sum()
paged_efficiency = np.array([
    live.sum() / (np.ceil(live / block) * block).sum()
    for block in block_sizes
])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.7))
ax.plot(block_sizes, 100 * paged_efficiency, "o-", label="paged")
ax.axhline(100 * contiguous_efficiency, color="0.35", ls="--",
           label="contiguous reservation")
ax.set(xlabel="block size (token slots)", ylabel="live-token efficiency (%)", ylim=(0, 102))
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 2: Illustrative allocation efficiency under variable request lengths. Paged allocation uses 16-token blocks.





These values are simulator outputs, not measurements from the vLLM paper. The qualitative trade-off is real: smaller blocks reduce internal fragmentation but increase block-table entries and kernel address-translation work.

title: A Paged KV-Cache Allocator, Built from First Principles
text:
Prefix sharing and copy-on-write
Paging makes sharing natural. Parallel samples from one prompt can point their logical prefix blocks to the same physical blocks. Maintain a reference count c_b for every physical block. A fork increments counts; releasing a request decrements them.
Appending to a shared partially filled block requires copy-on-write:
def append_with_cow(request, refcount, free_blocks, block_tokens):
    last = request.blocks[-1]
    offset = request.live_tokens % block_tokens
    if offset and refcount[last] > 1:
        replacement = free_blocks.pop()
        copy_block(last, replacement)  # device-to-device copy
        refcount[last] -= 1
        refcount[replacement] = 1
        request.blocks[-1] = replacement
    append_token_kv(request.blocks[-1], offset)
Full shared prefix blocks never need copying. Only the block currently being extended can trigger copy-on-write. This supports parallel sampling, beam search, and shared system prompts with the same mechanism.

title: A Paged KV-Cache Allocator, Built from First Principles
text:
Scheduling consequences
Better allocation increases the feasible batch size, but a production server must also decide which requests enter a batch and how to recover under pressure. Swapping cache blocks to host memory preserves work but consumes interconnect bandwidth. Recomputation discards blocks and rebuilds them with a prefill pass, trading compute for storage.
The vLLM paper reports near-zero KV-cache waste and 2 to 4 times higher throughput at comparable latency than the evaluated baselines (Kwon et al. 2023). The gain comes from the system built around the allocator, not address translation alone. Larger effective batches improve GPU utilization, while prefix sharing avoids duplicate storage.

title: A Paged KV-Cache Allocator, Built from First Principles
A Paged KV-Cache Allocator, Built from First Principles
text:
Limitations
This simulator counts token slots. Real systems allocate per layer, shard tensors across devices, align blocks for kernels, and synchronize allocator state with asynchronous execution. Kernel layout can also favor a block size that is not optimal under a pure fragmentation metric.
Still, the model captures the essential systems insight: once persistent state has irregular lifetimes, a tensor is not only a numerical object. It is also a dynamically allocated resource.

title: A Paged KV-Cache Allocator, Built from First Principles
text:
References


Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, et al. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.

Method
I prefer primary sources and explicit assumptions. When a result comes from a paper, the page cites it. When a graph comes from code, the code is included or described closely enough to reproduce it. When a number is illustrative rather than measured on real hardware, it is labelled as such.
The aim is not to compress a topic into a list of facts. It is to expose the mechanism: what is computed, why the equation has that form, where the memory goes, and under which conditions the method stops helping.

title: The Geometry of Rotary Position Embeddings
text:
Self-attention is permutation equivariant. If the rows of Q, K, and V are permuted together, the output rows are permuted in the same way. A language model therefore needs an additional structure that distinguishes token order.
Rotary position embedding, usually called RoPE, inserts that structure by rotating query and key coordinates (Su et al. 2024). The construction is small enough to fit in a few lines of code, but its real value is algebraic: absolute positions become relative offsets inside the attention dot product.

title: The Geometry of Rotary Position Embeddings
text:
A two-dimensional representation of position
For one coordinate pair, define

R(m\theta)=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos(m\theta)&-\sin(m\theta)\\
\sin(m\theta)& \cos(m\theta)
\end{bmatrix}.

At position m, RoPE maps q\mapsto R(m\theta)q and k\mapsto R(m\theta)k. Orthogonality and the group law R(a)^\top R(b)=R(b-a) give

\langle R(m\theta)q,R(n\theta)k\rangle
=q^\top R((n-m)\theta)k.
\tag{1}
The inputs carry absolute angles, but the logit depends only on n-m. Equation Equation 1 is the core of RoPE.
For even dimension d, the complete operator is block diagonal:

R_{\Theta,m}=\operatorname{diag}
\left(R(m\theta_0),R(m\theta_1),\ldots,R(m\theta_{d/2-1})\right),

with the conventional schedule

\theta_i=b^{-2i/d},\qquad b=10{,}000.

The first pairs rotate quickly and resolve nearby offsets. Later pairs rotate slowly and provide coarse phase information over larger distances.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

d = 64
base = 10_000
pair_ids = np.array([0, 8, 16, 24])
theta = base ** (-2 * pair_ids / d)
offset = np.arange(0, 4097)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(8, 5), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, i, frequency in zip(axes.flat, pair_ids, theta):
    ax.plot(offset, np.cos(offset * frequency), lw=1.1)
    ax.set_title(fr"pair $i={i}$, period $\approx {2*np.pi/frequency:.0f}$")
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
for ax in axes[-1]:
    ax.set_xlabel("relative offset")
for ax in axes[:, 0]:
    ax.set_ylabel("cosine phase")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Cosine phase across relative offsets for four RoPE frequency bands at head dimension 64.





The schedule is not a collection of position counters. Each pair is periodic and therefore ambiguous on its own. Position is represented by the joint phase across all pairs.

title: The Geometry of Rotary Position Embeddings
text:
Complex notation exposes the mechanism
Identify a coordinate pair (x_{2i},x_{2i+1}) with the complex number z_i=x_{2i}+\mathrm{i}x_{2i+1}. Rotation becomes multiplication:

z_i^{(m)}=z_i e^{\mathrm{i}m\theta_i}.

The real part of the Hermitian product between a rotated query and key contains

\operatorname{Re}\left(q_i\overline{k_i}e^{\mathrm{i}(m-n)\theta_i}\right).

This makes two facts visible. First, relative position modulates content similarity rather than adding an independent bias. Second, the model can learn how much each frequency matters by shaping q_i\overline{k_i} through the projection matrices.

title: The Geometry of Rotary Position Embeddings
text:
A vectorized implementation
import numpy as np

def apply_rope(x: np.ndarray, positions: np.ndarray, base: float = 10_000.0):
    """Rotate x with shape [sequence, heads, head_dim]."""
    d = x.shape[-1]
    assert d % 2 == 0
    inv_freq = base ** (-np.arange(0, d, 2) / d)
    angle = positions[:, None] * inv_freq[None, :]
    cos, sin = np.cos(angle)[:, None, :], np.sin(angle)[:, None, :]

    even, odd = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]
    out = np.empty_like(x)
    out[..., 0::2] = even * cos - odd * sin
    out[..., 1::2] = even * sin + odd * cos
    return out
Real kernels often use a rotate_half formulation or interleave dimensions differently. The pairing convention may vary, but queries and keys must use the same convention.

title: The Geometry of Rotary Position Embeddings
text:
Why extrapolation is difficult
RoPE defines angles at every integer position, so it is mechanically valid beyond the training length. That does not imply reliable extrapolation. At longer contexts, the model encounters phase combinations and attention distances absent during training.
For a training limit L, frequency pair i completes

c_i(L)=\frac{L\theta_i}{2\pi}

cycles. High-frequency pairs have observed many cycles and mostly encode local relative structure. Low-frequency pairs may not have completed one cycle, so they behave more like smooth absolute coordinates. Uniformly compressing every frequency changes both regimes, including the local phases the model already learned.

pair = np.arange(d // 2)
inv_freq = base ** (-2 * pair / d)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
for length in (2048, 32768):
    ax.semilogy(pair, length * inv_freq / (2 * np.pi), marker="o", ms=3,
                label=f"context {length:,}")
ax.axhline(1, color="0.5", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set(xlabel="coordinate-pair index", ylabel="completed rotations")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 2: Number of rotations observed by each coordinate pair at context lengths 2,048 and 32,768.





Changing the base b stretches the slow end of the spectrum. Position interpolation scales every position before rotation. More elaborate context-extension methods separate frequency bands because the pairs above and below the one-cycle boundary play different roles.

title: The Geometry of Rotary Position Embeddings
text:
Numerical and implementation details
RoPE preserves vector norms in exact arithmetic because every block is orthogonal. This provides a useful unit test:

\|R_{\Theta,m}x\|_2=\|x\|_2.

It also preserves a strict relative-position identity. For random q,k,m,n, the following quantities should agree:
left = np.dot(rotate(q, m), rotate(k, n))
right = np.dot(q, rotate(k, n - m))
np.testing.assert_allclose(left, right, rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-6)
For long contexts, compute the trigonometric tables with care. Low-precision angle formation can lose phase accuracy before the final vectors are cast to the model dtype. Many implementations form frequencies or angles in FP32 even when attention runs in BF16 or FP16.

title: The Geometry of Rotary Position Embeddings
text:
What RoPE buys
RoPE does not make attention cheaper. It gives attention a translation-compatible positional structure with no learned position table and no additive relative-bias matrix. Its popularity comes from that clean interface: rotate Q and K, leave V unchanged, and preserve the rest of the attention kernel.
The price is spectral. Context length, base frequency, scaling rule, and the distribution of training positions are coupled. Extending context is therefore a change to the geometry seen by the model, not merely an increase in an array bound.

title: The Geometry of Rotary Position Embeddings
text:
References


Su, Jianlin, Yu Lu, Shengfeng Pan, Ahmed Murtadha, Bo Wen, and Yunfeng Liu. 2024. “RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding.” Neurocomputing 568: 127063. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neucom.2023.127063.

title: FlashAttention Is an IO Algorithm
text:
The standard account of attention starts with an n\times n matrix. That is mathematically convenient and computationally misleading. A GPU does not pay only for arithmetic. It also pays to move every intermediate between high-bandwidth memory, caches, registers, and on-chip SRAM.
FlashAttention keeps the exact attention function but changes its evaluation schedule so the quadratic score and probability matrices are never written to high-bandwidth memory (Dao et al. 2022). The central technique is an online softmax that can be updated one tile at a time.

title: FlashAttention Is an IO Algorithm
section: The traffic in a literal implementation
text:
The traffic in a literal implementation
For one head,

S=QK^\top,\qquad P=\operatorname{softmax}(S),\qquad O=PV.

A conventional sequence of kernels writes S to HBM, reads it for softmax, writes P, then reads P for the second matrix multiplication. Both intermediates contain n^2 elements. Kernel fusion can remove some round trips, but S and P still exceed on-chip capacity at useful sequence lengths.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

n = 2 ** np.arange(8, 18)
d = 128
score_mib = n**2 * 2 / 2**20
qkv_mib = 3 * n * d * 2 / 2**20

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
ax.loglog(n, score_mib, "o-", label=r"one $n\times n$ matrix")
ax.loglog(n, qkv_mib, "o-", label=r"$Q,K,V$ at $d=128$")
ax.set(xlabel="sequence length", ylabel="storage (MiB)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(which="both", alpha=0.18)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Storage for one materialized attention matrix at FP16, compared with one linear-size QKV working set at head dimension 128.





At n=16{,}384, a single FP16 score matrix for one head and one batch element occupies 512 MiB. A model with many heads cannot retain all such matrices without aggressive memory management.

title: FlashAttention Is an IO Algorithm
text:
Softmax can be streamed exactly
For a row of logits x_1,\ldots,x_j, maintain the running maximum and exponential sum

m_j=\max_{i\le j}x_i,
\qquad
\ell_j=\sum_{i\le j}e^{x_i-m_j}.

When a new block B arrives, let

m_B=\max_{x\in B}x,qquad
\ell_B=\sum_{x\in B}e^{x-m_B},qquad
m'=\max(m_j,m_B).

The combined normalizer is

\ell'=e^{m_j-m'}\ell_j+e^{m_B-m'}\ell_B.
\tag{1}
For attention, maintain an unnormalized value accumulator

\widetilde{o}_j=\sum_{i\le j}e^{x_i-m_j}v_i.

It updates by the same rescaling:

\widetilde{o}'=e^{m_j-m'}\widetilde{o}_j
+e^{m_B-m'}\sum_{x_i\in B}e^{x_i-m_B}v_i,
\qquad o=\frac{\widetilde{o}'}{\ell'}.
\tag{2}
Equations Equation 1 and Equation 2 are exact apart from floating-point rounding. They let a kernel load a query tile, stream over key and value tiles, and retain only row statistics and a partial output on chip.
import numpy as np

def tiled_attention(q, k, v, block=64):
    """Reference implementation for one query vector, not a fast kernel."""
    scale = q.shape[-1] ** -0.5
    m = -np.inf
    ell = 0.0
    acc = np.zeros(v.shape[-1], dtype=np.float64)

    for start in range(0, len(k), block):
        kb = k[start:start + block]
        vb = v[start:start + block]
        logits = kb @ q * scale
        block_max = logits.max()
        new_max = max(m, block_max)

        old_scale = np.exp(m - new_max)
        weights = np.exp(logits - new_max)
        acc = old_scale * acc + weights @ vb
        ell = old_scale * ell + weights.sum()
        m = new_max

    return acc / ell
This Python version exposes the recurrence but does not provide the speedup. Performance comes from mapping tiles to GPU thread blocks and using tensor-core matrix multiplications while intermediates remain in SRAM or registers.

title: FlashAttention Is an IO Algorithm
text:
Tiling the full matrix
Partition Q into row tiles Q_i and K,V into column tiles K_j,V_j. For each Q_i:

Load Q_i once into on-chip memory.
Stream through (K_j,V_j) pairs.
Compute Q_iK_j^\top as a small tile.
Update each row’s (m,\ell,\widetilde{o}) state.
Write the final O_i and log-sum-exp statistics.

The algorithm still performs dense attention arithmetic. Its gain comes from reducing expensive HBM transactions. The original analysis gives an HBM access complexity of

\Theta\!\left(\frac{n^2d^2}{M}\right),

for SRAM capacity M, over the relevant range of tile sizes, compared with quadratic intermediate traffic in the standard schedule (Dao et al. 2022).

title: FlashAttention Is an IO Algorithm
text:
Backward by recomputation
Ordinary autodiff saves S or P because the backward pass needs probabilities. FlashAttention stores the output and row-wise log-sum-exp, then recomputes score tiles during backward.
Recomputation adds FLOPs but removes the quadratic saved activation. On modern accelerators, this trade can be faster because matrix multiplication is efficient while repeated HBM traffic is expensive. This is a selective checkpointing strategy guided by the memory hierarchy.

title: FlashAttention Is an IO Algorithm
text:
FlashAttention-2 changes the work partition
The first algorithm removed the primary IO bottleneck but reached only 25 to 40 percent of A100 peak throughput. FlashAttention-2 targets utilization (Dao 2023):

It delays output normalization to reduce non-matrix FLOPs.
It parallelizes over sequence tiles in addition to batch and heads, improving occupancy when batch size or head count is small.
It partitions Q across warps while sharing K and V, avoiding the shared-memory reductions induced by splitting K.

The paper reports 50 to 73 percent of theoretical A100 peak and up to 225 TFLOP/s for GPT-style training (Dao 2023). Those numbers depend on model shape and hardware. They are not a universal speed multiplier.

title: FlashAttention Is an IO Algorithm
text:
Arithmetic intensity and the roofline
A roofline model bounds performance by

\text{throughput}\le
\min\left(\text{peak FLOP/s},\;
\text{bandwidth}\times\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes moved}}\right).

Changing the evaluation order raises arithmetic intensity by doing more useful work per byte transferred from HBM. Once the kernel crosses into the compute-bound regime, further reductions in traffic yield less benefit and work partitioning becomes decisive.
This explains an apparently paradoxical result: an algorithm may execute more arithmetic through recomputation and still finish sooner.

title: FlashAttention Is an IO Algorithm
text:
Boundaries
FlashAttention does not make dense attention asymptotically linear in compute. It makes memory usage linear and reduces IO. Dense arithmetic remains quadratic in sequence length. It also does not replace the KV cache during autoregressive decoding. FlashAttention optimizes the attention kernel; KV-cache paging manages persistent state across requests.
That distinction is worth keeping. Similar words such as memory-efficient can refer to activation memory, persistent cache capacity, allocator fragmentation, or bandwidth traffic. These are different constraints with different remedies.

title: FlashAttention Is an IO Algorithm
text:
References


Dao, Tri. 2023. “FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2307.08691. https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08691.


Dao, Tri, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra, and Christopher Ré. 2022. “FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35: 16344–59. https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135.
